opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a fair question, and honestly I think I was wrong in a pretty interesting way. Early in my career, a lot of my work was on structured prediction: dynamic programming, dual decomposition, Lagrangian relaxation, the idea that language has this rich latent structure like parse trees, alignments, and segmentations, and that the right way to do NLP was to model that structure explicitly and then do hard combinatorial inference over it. I really believed that even as neural networks came in, they'd mostly be the scoring function, and the interesting algorithmic work would still be in the inference layer on top.

What actually happened is that scale and very generic architectures just absorbed most of that. A big transformer trained on enough text doesn't need you to hand it a CKY parser. It learns whatever internal representations it needs, and the inference at test time became, for a long while, just left-to-right sampling. That was humbling. A lot of the beautiful machinery I cared about turned out not to be necessary for the headline results.

But I don't think the story ends there, and that's the part I find exciting now. The core questions never went away: how do you search over a combinatorial space of outputs, how do you trade off compute at test time against quality, how do you reason about distributions over structured objects. They've come back in a different form. When people talk about test-time compute, reasoning traces, search over chains of thought, verifiers, best-of-n, or reinforcement learning on long generations, that's inference again. It's just that the "structure" is now sequences the model itself produces rather than syntax trees we designed.

So my updated view is something like this: I was wrong that explicit linguistic structure plus exact inference would be central. I was maybe right that inference, meaning how you spend computation to get from a model to a good answer, would be central. The lesson for me was to be less attached to the specific formalism and more attached to the underlying problem. And to be a bit more humble about betting against scale.

r001.rationale: The response traces a shift from explicit structured inference to scale-driven learning, then describes inference returning in forms such as test-time search and compute.

r002.rationale: Rush explicitly says, “I was wrong” about explicit linguistic structure and exact inference remaining central.

r003.rationale: The response says generic architectures trained on enough text absorbed much of the work and that this was humbling, acknowledging that scale and learning from data mattered more than he expected.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I think I was wrong, at least about the form it would take. When I was coming up, a lot of my work was on structured prediction, on things like dependency parsing with dynamic programming, CKY, inference over latent trees. The bet was that language has this rich combinatorial structure, and that we'd need explicit algorithms to search over it. That felt like the center of the field. The modeling was almost secondary to figuring out how to do inference efficiently.

And then transformers came along, and for a while it looked like all of that was just gone. You had a big dense model, you ran it forward, you took the argmax. There wasn't any interesting inference happening, or so it seemed. I'll admit there were a few years where I felt like a lot of what I knew had become a historical curiosity.

What's interesting to me now is that inference has come back, just not in the shape I expected. Look at what people are doing with decoding: chain of thought, sampling many candidates, verifiers, tree search over reasoning steps, speculative decoding. That is inference. It's search over a structured space, with a model giving you scores. The difference is that the structure isn't something I wrote down as a grammar. It emerges from the model, and the search happens in the token space rather than over parse trees I designed.

So my view has shifted from "inference is central because language has structure we must encode" to "inference is central because test-time computation matters, and how you spend it is a real design choice." That's a humbler version of the belief. The intuitions from the old world, about dynamic programming, about trading compute for accuracy, about marginalizing over latent variables, those still turn out to be useful. The specific commitments about which structures matter mostly didn't survive.

If I'm being honest about the lesson, it's that I overestimated how much of the structure needed to be hand-specified, and underestimated how much the model would learn on its own. But I think I'd push back a little on the idea that the field just became "scale a transformer." The people getting the most out of these models today are thinking very carefully about what happens at inference time. So the belief was wrong in its details, but the instinct wasn't entirely off.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts hand-specified inference with learned structure and discusses test-time computation, but does not describe NLP history as alternating between learning and inference.

r002.rationale: Rush says he overestimated how much structure needed to be hand-specified, while maintaining that inference remains central. He does not acknowledge overestimating inference’s future importance.

r003.rationale: The response says he underestimated how much structure models would learn, but does not mention NLP improving by learning from increasing amounts of data.

astra-6.text: I think I was wrong about that. My intuition was that language was so structured that we would need fairly sophisticated inference procedures to produce good outputs. And I spent a lot of time thinking about those procedures. What surprised me was how much of that work could be absorbed into learning a better model. Once the model gets good enough, relatively simple decoding can take you much further than I expected. That doesn’t mean inference is irrelevant, but I no longer think the complexity has to live where I originally thought it did.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts complex inference with learning a better model, but does not describe NLP history as alternating emphasis between them.

r002.rationale: Rush says he was wrong to expect sophisticated inference procedures to remain necessary and explains that better models absorbed much of that work.

r003.rationale: The response credits improvement to learning a better model, but does not say that NLP improved by learning from increasing amounts of data.

sol-6.1.text: I think I was wrong about how central it would be. Earlier in my career, I thought the hard part of NLP was going to be figuring out how to do inference over these complicated structured spaces. We put a lot of our effort into that. What surprised me was how much of that complexity you could move into learning, and then get very far with a relatively simple decoding procedure. I still find inference interesting, but I’m much less convinced that the particular kinds of structured inference I worked on are essential to building useful language systems.

r001.rationale: It contrasts complex inference with learning, but does not describe NLP's history as alternating between the two emphases.

r002.rationale: Rush says he was wrong about how central complex inference would be and is now less convinced it is essential.

r003.rationale: The response says complexity could be moved into learning, but does not mention underestimating improvement from increasing amounts of data.
